identification.summary: China-based human-operated ransomware actor that Microsoft (as DEV-0401) describes as running every stage of the attack itself, from initial access to ransomware development, rather than using an affiliate model or buying access [S1][S9]. It gains access by exploiting unpatched internet-facing software and frequently rebrands its ransomware payloads, so payload-based reporting can make it look like several different groups [S1]. Secureworks (BRONZE STARLIGHT) and MITRE assess that the ransomware may be a smokescreen and that the underlying motive may be intellectual-property theft or espionage rather than profit [S3][S9].
identification.firstObserved: Secureworks coverage: active since early 2021 [S4]. MITRE: active since at least 2021 [S9]. Microsoft's DEV-0401 payload timeline begins in 2021 [S1].
identification.notes: Microsoft name: Cinnamon Tempest (formerly DEV-0401); Microsoft's DEV-0401 reporting calls the group China-based [S1][S9]. MITRE tracks it as G1021 with associated names DEV-0401, Emperor Dragonfly and BRONZE STARLIGHT [S9]. Emperor Dragonfly is Sygnia's name; Sygnia linked the Night Sky and Cheerscrypt ransomware to it [S6]. Ransomware brands reported for the cluster: LockFile, AtomSilo, Rook, Night Sky, Pandora (Secureworks), LockBit 2.0 (Microsoft) and Cheerscrypt (Sygnia) [S1][S3][S6].

attribution.sponsor: China-based; no public source reviewed names a specific PRC government sponsor or unit [S1][S3]. Secureworks and SentinelLabs describe the actor as China-linked or China-aligned and suggest espionage aims, but neither ties it to a named state organization [S3][S7].
attribution.confidence: Microsoft states DEV-0401 is 'confirmed to be a China-based activity group' [S1]. Secureworks CTU assesses with moderate confidence that BRONZE STARLIGHT is located in China and that ransomware may be a smokescreen for IP theft or espionage [S3]. SentinelLabs says indicators point to BRONZE STARLIGHT but the exact grouping remains unclear given interconnected Chinese APT relationships [S7]. No government attribution was found.
attribution.basis: Microsoft telemetry of the full attack lifecycle and payload history [S1][S2]; Secureworks analysis of HUI Loader, which it has only seen used by likely China-based groups, plus PlugX and victimology [S3][S4]; Sygnia incident response linking Night Sky and Cheerscrypt TTPs and Chinese-language open-source tooling [S6]; MITRE's synthesis of victimology, short ransomware lifespans and use of malware tied to government-sponsored groups [S9].

objectives: Overtly, ransomware extortion with name-and-shame leak sites [S1][S3]. Secureworks and MITRE assess that the real objective may be intellectual-property theft or cyber-espionage, citing victimology, the short lifespan of each ransomware brand and the use of state-associated malware [S3][S9]. SentinelLabs reporting on gambling-sector intrusions points to collection on Southeast Asian gambling operations of interest to China [S7].

sectors: Aerospace and defense (defense division of an Indian conglomerate) [S5]
Organizations running unpatched VMware Horizon, Exchange, ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus or Confluence (opportunistic) [S1][S2]
targeting.notes: Victim list comes from secondary summaries of the Secureworks report, not the primary text [S4][S5]. Secureworks notes the ransomware tended to hit a small number of organizations over a short period before each brand was dropped [S4]. Initial access is driven by exposed vulnerable software, so victims may partly reflect opportunity rather than tasking [S1].

capabilities.summary: Exploits unpatched public-facing software, including Exchange, ManageEngine ADSelfService Plus, Confluence and Log4j 2 (CVE-2021-44228) in VMware Horizon, and typically obtains elevated credentials at initial access [S1][S2]. Uses Cobalt Strike, often launched by DLL search-order hijacking; around June 2022 Microsoft saw it begin replacing Cobalt Strike with Sliver [S1]. Uses the custom HUI Loader to decrypt and run Cobalt Strike and PlugX [S3]. Moves laterally with a customized Impacket wmiexec.py and deploys ransomware from batch files via Group Policy, often staged in the domain controller NETLOGON share, which requires domain-admin-level credentials [S1]. Exfiltrates with Rclone to Mega cloud storage and runs ransomware against both Windows and VMware ESXi [S6]. Ransomware is rebuilt from leaked code (Babuk-derived Rook, Night Sky and Pandora) or bought in, as with LockBit 2.0 [S1][S3]. SentinelOne linked to DEV-0401 a LockBit intrusion that side-loaded Cobalt Strike through a signed VMware utility and evaded EDR, ETW and AMSI [S8]. Gambling-sector intrusions attributed to the group used DLL hijacking of Adobe, Edge and McAfee executables and a likely stolen code-signing certificate [S7].

campaigns.name: LockFile and AtomSilo ransomware operations
campaigns.summary: Secureworks reports LockFile and AtomSilo as the group's first ransomware strains, followed by Babuk-derived families [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Night Sky via Log4j in VMware Horizon
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports DEV-0401 exploiting CVE-2021-44228 on internet-facing VMware Horizon from as early as 4 January 2022, leading to Night Sky ransomware [S2].

campaigns.name: Cheerscrypt intrusion (Emperor Dragonfly)
campaigns.summary: Sygnia investigated a January 2022 intrusion that began with Log4Shell on VMware Horizon and ended with Rclone exfiltration to Mega and Cheerscrypt encryption, linking Cheerscrypt to Night Sky [S6].

campaigns.name: Pandora ransomware deployments
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed Pandora deployed mainly through unpatched VMware Horizon systems vulnerable to Log4j 2 [S1].

campaigns.name: Shift to LockBit 2.0
campaigns.summary: Microsoft reports that DEV-0401 began deploying LockBit 2.0 in April 2022 [S1]. SentinelOne later tied to DEV-0401 a LockBit intrusion that side-loaded Cobalt Strike through VMwareXferlogs.exe [S8].

campaigns.name: Cobalt Strike to Sliver transition
campaigns.summary: Microsoft observed DEV-0401 starting to replace Cobalt Strike with Sliver around 6 June 2022 [S1].

campaigns.name: Secureworks HUI Loader disclosure
campaigns.summary: Secureworks publicly attributes the HUI Loader ransomware cluster to BRONZE STARLIGHT and assesses the ransomware may be a smokescreen [S3][S4].

campaigns.name: Southeast Asian gambling sector intrusions
campaigns.summary: SentinelLabs reports Cobalt Strike delivered through DLL hijacking against Southeast Asian gambling companies, with indicators pointing to BRONZE STARLIGHT, and links it to ESET's Operation ChattyGoblin [S7].

campaigns.name: RA World ransomware attack (low-confidence link)
campaigns.summary: Symantec, as reported by BleepingComputer, describes an RA World attack on a South Asian software firm that used PlugX and the NPS proxy tool, which Bronze Starlight has used before. Unit 42 linked RA World to Emperor Dragonfly/Bronze Starlight only with low confidence [S10].

diamond.adversary: China-based group tracked as Cinnamon Tempest / DEV-0401 / BRONZE STARLIGHT / Emperor Dragonfly that runs the whole intrusion and ransomware chain itself [S1][S3][S6][S9].
diamond.capability: N-day exploitation (Exchange, ManageEngine, Confluence, Log4j/VMware Horizon); HUI Loader, PlugX, Cobalt Strike, Sliver, Impacket, Rclone; Babuk-derived and purchased ransomware such as LockBit 2.0; Windows and ESXi encryptors [S1][S2][S3][S6].
diamond.infrastructure: Compromised internet-facing servers used for entry; Mega cloud storage for exfiltration; leak sites that sometimes led to default web pages; Alibaba-hosted staging and a likely stolen code-signing certificate in gambling-sector activity [S1][S6][S7].
diamond.victim: Pharmaceutical, electronics manufacturing, aerospace/defense, media and legal organizations in the US, Brazil, Lithuania, Japan and India; Southeast Asian gambling companies [S5][S7].
diamond.socioPolitical: Vendors assess the ransomware may cover IP theft or espionage that serves Chinese interests [S3][S9]. SentinelLabs ties gambling-sector targeting to China's interest in the region following its Macao gambling crackdown [S7].
diamond.technology: Unpatched VMware Horizon (Log4j), Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine servers; Active Directory and Group Policy used for mass deployment; VMware ESXi hypervisors [S1][S2][S6].

gaps: Primary Secureworks, Sygnia, SentinelLabs, Symantec and MITRE pages could not be fetched (DNS or host blocked). Their content is taken from mirrors (Sophos for Secureworks), press releases, news coverage and search-result summaries; validate against the originals.
Microsoft's threat-actor naming page (learn.microsoft.com) could not be opened to confirm the DEV-0401 to Cinnamon Tempest mapping directly; the mapping relies on the record's import and MITRE [S9].
No public government attribution or named PRC sponsor or unit was found.
Whether the ransomware is a smokescreen for espionage is an analytic judgment by Secureworks and MITRE, not a demonstrated fact; Microsoft treats the group as a ransomware operator [S1][S3][S9].

Cluster boundaries: Secureworks attributes a separate HUI Loader cluster aimed at Japanese IP theft to BRONZE RIVERSIDE (APT10-linked), not BRONZE STARLIGHT [S3]. SentinelLabs says the exact grouping of the gambling-sector activity is unclear [S7]. The RA World link rests on Unit 42 low-confidence attribution and Symantec hypothesis, and the PlugX variant was tied to Fireant/Mustang Panda [S10].
SentinelOne's LockBit side-loading case was linked to DEV-0401 after the fact; the details of that linkage were not reviewed in primary form [S8].

The TeamT5 Black Hat Asia 2022 talk ('To Loot or Not to Loot') on state-nexus attacks against online entertainment is cited in the actor record, but its slides were not reviewed and its link to this specific cluster is unconfirmed.
No public reporting confirming activity attributed to Cinnamon Tempest by name after 2023 was found, apart from the low-confidence RA World link.
The share of victims by sector or country, and any data stolen for espionage purposes, are not public in the sources gathered.

implications.jipoe: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. STEP 1 (OE): Internet-facing VMware Horizon, Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine servers, along with Active Directory and domain controllers (NETLOGON and Group Policy), are key cyber terrain. So are ESXi hypervisors hosting mission systems [S1][S2][S6]. STEP 2 (effects): N-day exploitation gives the actor elevated credentials at entry, which shortens the time to domain-wide ransomware deployment. ESXi encryption raises the impact on virtualized infrastructure [S1][S6]. STEP 3 (adversary template): Exploit an exposed server; load Cobalt Strike or Sliver through DLL hijacking or HUI Loader; move laterally with Impacket wmiexec; exfiltrate with Rclone to Mega; deploy a short-lived ransomware brand by GPO batch script [S1][S3][S6]. STEP 4: MLCOA is opportunistic exploitation of unpatched perimeter services in defense-industrial, aerospace, electronics or pharma networks, followed by data theft and ransomware that may mask collection [S1][S3][S5]. MDCOA is domain-wide encryption of Windows and ESXi supporting mission-critical systems after IP exfiltration, with the ransomware masking espionage and misdirecting incident response [S3][S6]. Candidate indicators: Log4j exploitation attempts against Horizon; signed binaries (VMware, Adobe, McAfee, Edge) loading unexpected DLLs; renamed wmiexec output files; Rclone or Mega traffic; new batch files in NETLOGON or GPO changes [S1][S6][S7][S8].
implications.jcc2: Analyst assessment derived from cited sources; validate before use. Situational awareness: track exposure and patch status of Horizon, Exchange, Confluence and ManageEngine instances across DODIN and DIB partner enclaves, since this actor relies on known vulnerabilities rather than bought access [S1][S2]. Authorities: a ransomware event linked to this cluster may be espionage rather than crime, so plan early coordination between DCO, counterintelligence and law-enforcement channels instead of treating it purely as criminal extortion [S3][S9]. Mission assurance: protect domain controllers, Group Policy and ESXi management planes, and keep offline backups of virtualized mission systems [S1][S6]. Coordination: share indicators with DIB and partner-nation CERTs in affected sectors and regions (US, Brazil, Lithuania, Japan, India, Southeast Asia), and deconflict cluster names (DEV-0401, BRONZE STARLIGHT, Emperor Dragonfly) when fusing vendor reporting [S5][S7][S9].

provenance.importedSummary: BRONZE STARLIGHT has been active since mid 2021 and targets organizations globally across a range of industry verticals. The group leverages HUI Loader to load Cobalt Strike and PlugX payloads for command and control. CTU researchers have observed BRONZE STARLIGHT deploying ransomware to compromised networks as part of name-and-shame ransomware schemes, and posted victim names to leak sites. CTU researchers assess with moderate confidence that BRONZE STARLIGHT is located in China based on observed tradecraft, including the use of HUI Loader and PlugX which are associated with China-based threat group activity. It is plausible that BRONZE STARLIGHT deploys ransomware as a smokescreen rather than for financial gain, with the underlying motivation of stealing intellectual property theft or conducting espionage.
